name: Decline Sit-Up
description: The decline sit-up is performed on a decline bench with the feet secured at the high end, increasing the range of motion and gravitational challenge compared to a flat-surface sit-up. The decline angle lengthens the rectus abdominis at the starting position, providing a greater stretch-to-contraction range that is not achievable on a flat surface. Hip flexors contribute significantly at the lower portion of the movement, while the rectus abdominis dominates during the final degrees of spinal flexion at the top.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the decline bench with feet secured under the ankle pads, knees bent. Cross arms over the chest or place fingertips behind the ears.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench to a moderate decline (20–40°). Ensure the ankle pads firmly hold the feet without causing ankle discomfort.
steps: Step 1: Begin lying fully extended on the bench. Engage the core.
Step 2: Curl the chin toward the chest, then lift the torso by sequentially contracting the abs and flexing the spine.
Step 3: Continue rising until the torso is fully upright or slightly past vertical.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to the starting position with control, allowing the spine to extend fully against the bench.
Step 5: Avoid jerking the neck or using momentum from the arms.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the way up. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Pulling the neck with the hands behind the head — this compresses the cervical spine
Using a momentum bounce at the bottom rather than a controlled eccentric
safety_considerations: Those with lower-back issues should consult a clinician before performing decline sit-ups due to substantial lumbar loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom to full upright (or slightly forward) at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-0. Slow and controlled. No bouncing at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Lead with the chest, not the neck
Control the way down — don't drop
